0.title: Following Jesus as a Teenager
0.essay:
The teenage years are when you begin to decide for yourself who you are, what you believe and how you will live. That makes them exciting, confusing and sometimes painful. This study is for you if you are about thirteen to eighteen.

The big questions

Teenagers ask the biggest questions there are. Is any of this true, or did I just grow up with it? Who am I? What do I do with my body, my desires and my feelings? Why do I feel so anxious? How do I live for Christ when hardly anyone else at school does? Scripture does not avoid these questions, and neither will we.

God has always used young people. Joseph, David, Daniel and Mary were all teenagers or close to it when God called them. Paul told Timothy, “Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity” (1 Timothy 4:12).

The chapters

1. Is This Faith Mine?: owning your faith, doubts and assurance. 2. Identity, Body and Image: who you are in a world of filters. 3. Sex, Dating and Purity. 4. Friends, Parents and Pressure: including alcohol and drugs. 5. Anxiety, Sadness and Stress. 6. Living for Christ at School and Online: witness, hard questions and the future.

For reflection

Which of these chapters feels most urgent for you right now? Start there if you want to.

1.title: Is This Faith Mine?
1.essay:
Growing up in a Christian home is a gift. But at some point you must ask: do I believe this, or just my parents? Faith cannot be inherited like eye colour. Each person must come to Christ for themselves.

Second-hand faith

Many teenagers who grew up in church drift away in their late teens. Often it is not because they were argued out of their faith, but because it was never truly theirs. They knew the stories and the songs, but not the Saviour. Jesus warned that some people honour him with their lips, while their hearts are far from him (Matthew 15:8).

Coming to Christ

Owning your faith does not mean inventing something new. It means personally turning from sin and trusting Christ, who died for your sins and rose again. “But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12). You may remember a day when this happened, or you may have believed for as long as you can remember. Either way, the question is: do you trust him now?

Doubts

Doubt is not the opposite of faith. Unbelief, a settled refusal to trust, is. Many great Christians went through seasons of serious doubt. Thomas would not believe until he saw, and Jesus met him and showed him his wounds (John 20:27). Bring your questions out into the open. Read good books, ask your pastor or youth leader, and keep praying, even if your prayers feel empty. Do not just quietly let go.

Assurance

How can you know you are a Christian? Not by how strongly you feel, which changes every day. Look to Christ’s promise: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). Then look for signs of new life: a love for God, a hatred of sin, a desire to obey, and love for other Christians (1 John 3:14). They will not be perfect, but they will be real.

Making it real

Faith grows when it is fed. Read the Bible for yourself, even a short passage each day. Pray in your own words. Get to know older Christians who are not your parents. Serve in church: helping with younger children or the music team. And be baptised, if you have come to trust Christ and have not yet been, as a public sign that you belong to him.

A Tuesday afternoon

Ben had gone to church every Sunday of his life. At sixteen, he realised he did not know if he believed any of it. He told his youth leader, who did not panic, but met him every other week to read Mark’s Gospel. Halfway through, Ben said, “I think I’ve never actually looked at Jesus before.”

For reflection

If your parents stopped believing tomorrow, would you still trust Christ? Why?

2.title: Identity, Body and Image
2.essay:
Teenagers face more pressure about image than any generation before them. Every photo can be filtered, compared and rated. The world says: you are what you look like, what you achieve and how you feel. The gospel says something better.

The pressure to look right

Social media shows you an endless stream of perfect bodies, faces and lives, most of them edited. It is no wonder many teenagers feel ugly or inadequate. “Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised” (Proverbs 31:30). God “looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). Your body is a good gift. Look after it, but do not worship it or hate it.

Who you are

Our culture says that you must discover and create your own identity, deep inside yourself. That is an exhausting job, and the answer keeps changing. Christianity says your identity is a gift: you are made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27), and, if you trust Christ, you are a child of God, forgiven and loved. “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (1 John 3:1). That is true on your best days and your worst.

Gender and sexuality questions

You may have friends who identify as gay, bisexual or transgender, or you may have questions about your own feelings. These are real and often painful questions, and they deserve care, not jokes. Scripture teaches that God made us “male and female” (Genesis 1:27), that our bodies are part of who we are, and that sex belongs in marriage between a man and a woman. It also teaches that every one of us has desires that are bent by sin, and that Jesus welcomes all who come to him.

If you are struggling with these feelings, you are not alone, and you are not beyond God’s love. Talk to a mature Christian you trust. Feelings are real, but they do not have the final word about who you are. Christ does. Be kind to friends who see things differently. You can love someone without agreeing with them.

Eating and the body

Some teenagers begin to control their eating, over-exercise or harm their bodies because of how they feel about themselves. If that is you, please tell someone today. It is not a sign of weakness to ask for help, and it can be dangerous to wait.

A Tuesday afternoon

Chloe noticed she felt worse every time she scrolled through her feed. She decided to delete one app for a month. At first she felt she was missing out. By the end of the month, she said she felt “like myself again,” and she had read the whole of John’s Gospel.

For reflection

Where do you go to find out whether you are acceptable? What would change if you believed what God says about you?

3.title: Sex, Dating and Purity
3.essay:
Sexual desire is not dirty. God made it, and he made it good. But because it is powerful, it needs a safe place. The Bible calls Christians to sexual purity, not because God is against pleasure, but because he is for our good.

A good gift

God created sex for marriage, as a way for a husband and wife to become “one flesh” (Genesis 2:24), to delight in each other and to have children. The Song of Songs celebrates it openly. So the Christian view of sex is not negative. It is high. It is precisely because sex is so precious that it should not be cheapened.

Purity

“For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor” (1 Thessalonians 4:3–4). Purity means keeping sex for marriage. But it also includes your thoughts and what you look at. Jesus said that looking at someone with lustful intent is adultery in the heart (Matthew 5:28).

That does not mean every attraction is sin. Noticing that someone is attractive, or feeling a pull of desire, is temptation, not lust. Lust is when you welcome it, feed it and fantasise. Jesus himself was tempted, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). The battle is in what you do next.

Pornography

Many teenagers see pornography before they are fourteen, often by accident at first. It is designed to be addictive, it exploits real people, and it trains you to see people as objects. If you are caught in it, you are not beyond help. Tell someone you trust, use filters, keep devices out of your bedroom at night, and remember that Christ forgives and changes. “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

Dating

The Bible does not mention dating, but it gives wisdom. Ask what a relationship is for. If you are years away from marriage, an exclusive relationship may bring more temptation and heartache than good. If you do date, date a Christian (1 Corinthians 7:39), keep physical boundaries well before the danger line, spend time in groups, and involve your parents. Do not let a relationship become the centre of your life.

Safety

No one has the right to pressure you into anything sexual, in person or online. If someone sends you explicit images, or asks you to send them, say no and tell an adult. Sending such images of anyone under eighteen is illegal. And if anyone has touched you in a way that is wrong, it is not your fault. Tell a trusted adult.

A Tuesday afternoon

Liam’s friends were sharing a link in a group chat. He knew what it was. He left the chat and messaged his youth leader: “Can we talk?” It was the first time he had told anyone about his struggle. It was also the first step to freedom.

For reflection

Is there anything about sex, dating or pornography that you are hiding? Who is one safe person you could tell?

4.title: Friends, Parents and Pressure
4.essay:
In your teens, friends become more important and parents can seem less so. That is part of growing up. But the people you choose to stand with will shape your life, and how you treat your parents still matters to God.

Choose your friends

“Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm” (Proverbs 13:20). Look for at least one or two friends who share your faith and will help you follow Christ. Be friendly to everyone, but be careful who you let shape your choices.

Peer pressure

The pressure to fit in can push you to do things you would never do alone: drink, take drugs, cheat, mock others or lie to your parents. “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent” (Proverbs 1:10). Decide ahead of time where your lines are, so that you do not have to decide in the moment. Have an exit plan, such as a parent you can text who will pick you up, no questions asked.

Alcohol and drugs

Scripture does not forbid alcohol for adults, but it warns strongly against drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18). For teenagers, it is usually illegal and especially harmful to a growing brain. Drugs carry even greater dangers, from addiction to death. Many people take them to escape pain or loneliness. If that is you, find someone to talk to. Christ offers a better escape: rest in him.

Your parents

The command to honour your father and mother (Exodus 20:12) does not end at thirteen. As you grow, it changes. You will make more of your own decisions, and you may disagree with your parents more. But you can still speak respectfully, listen to their advice, and obey them in the things that are theirs to decide. They are not perfect. Some parents are harsh, distant or not Christians. But honour does not depend on their perfection. And if a parent is abusing you, honour does not mean silence: tell another trusted adult.

Arguments at home

Arguments often get worse because both sides want to win. Try listening first and asking questions. “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger” (James 1:19). Apologise when you are wrong. You might be surprised how much freedom parents give a teenager who is honest with them.

A Tuesday afternoon

At a party, Zara’s friends began passing round a vape. She had already told her dad she might call. She sent him one word, and he arrived ten minutes later. He didn’t lecture her in the car. He just said, “I’m proud of you.”

For reflection

Who are the two or three friends who most shape you? Are they helping you follow Christ?

5.title: Anxiety, Sadness and Stress
5.essay:
Many teenagers today struggle with anxiety, low mood or stress. If you are one of them, you are not weak, and you are not alone. God is close to the hurting, and help is available.

Why so many are struggling

There are many reasons: exam pressure, social media, family problems, loneliness, lack of sleep, and the changes of growing up. Some anxiety and sadness is a normal part of life. But sometimes it becomes heavy and constant, and it begins to affect your sleep, eating, friendships and schoolwork. Then it is time to get help.

God is near

The Psalms are full of people who were anxious and sad. “Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him” (Psalm 42:5). God does not tell you to cheer up. He invites you to bring your feelings to him. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit” (Psalm 34:18).

Practical steps

Your body and soul are linked. Sleep, exercise, food and sunlight make a real difference. So does time away from screens. Talk to someone. Write down your worries and pray through them one by one. “Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4:6). Thanksgiving matters: name three good things each day.

Exams and the future

Exams can feel as if your whole future depends on them. Work hard; it honours God. But remember that God holds your future, not an exam board. Many people whose results disappointed them have gone on to serve God faithfully and happily.

When it is serious

If you are harming yourself, or thinking about ending your life, please tell someone today: a parent, a teacher, a pastor or a doctor. In the UK and Ireland you can call Samaritans at any time on 116 123, or in an emergency call 999 (112 in Europe, 911 in North America). Asking for help is not failure. It is wisdom. Your life is precious to God.

Helping a friend

If a friend tells you they are struggling or thinking of self-harm, listen, take it seriously, and tell a trusted adult, even if they ask you not to. You are not betraying them. You may be saving their life.

A Tuesday afternoon

Ethan had not slept properly for weeks before his exams. His mum noticed and sat with him at the kitchen table. They wrote down every worry, prayed through the list, and made a plan for sleep and revision. The worries did not vanish. But they became smaller once they were shared.

For reflection

What is weighing on you most right now? Tell God, and tell one person you trust.

6.title: Living for Christ at School and Online
6.essay:
You may be the only Christian in your class, or one of a few. That can feel lonely. It is also an opportunity. God has placed you there to be light, to answer questions and to show what Jesus is like.

Salt and light

Jesus said, “You are the light of the world… let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:14, 16). Most of your witness will not be preaching. It will be honesty, kindness, refusing to join in gossip, working hard and treating the outsider well.

Answering questions

Your friends may ask hard questions: How can a good God allow suffering? Hasn’t science disproved God? Why do you think Christianity is right and other religions are wrong? You don’t need to have every answer. “In your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15). Read a good book on these questions, and if you don’t know, say, “Good question. Let me find out.”

Online

Your online life is real life. Do not say things online you would not say face to face. Do not join in pile-ons, mockery or gossip. Ask whether your posts show the fruit of the Spirit. And remember that what you post can stay there for ever.

Your future

You may feel pressure to know what you will do with your life. God does not usually show the whole map at once. Seek to be faithful in what is in front of you: your studies, your family, your church. Develop your gifts. Ask wise people what they see in you. “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding” (Proverbs 3:5). Whatever you end up doing, you can do it for him.

Belong to a church

Don’t try to follow Christ alone. Be part of a church, not just a youth group. Get to know Christians of all ages. When school is hard, church is where you are reminded who you are.

A Tuesday afternoon

In a religious studies lesson, the teacher asked if anyone believed in the resurrection. Rosie put up her hand, nervously, and explained why. Afterwards, a classmate she barely knew asked her where she went to church. A month later, he came with her.

For reflection

Who at school or online might be watching how you live? What is one way you could let your light shine this week?
